script.opening: “(Mum) It’s his feet. They stink the house out, the skin’s peeling, and the cream from the chemist did nothing. He needs something stronger. And he won’t listen to a word I say.”

facts.text: Jo (mother) and Callum, 16, sitting side by side. Callum has his hood up, short answers, does not look at the camera.

Itchy, white soggy skin between the toes, cracked and peeling, for about two months. Both feet. No redness spreading up the foot, no swelling, no fever, no nail changes. Cream from the chemist used twice, then lost.
Same trainers and socks for days, showering “maybe twice a week”, up gaming until 3am, “grumpy”, not seeing his mates, quit Sunday football. She thinks he is “just being a teenager” and lazy.

facts.topic: Only when seen alone and made safe
facts.text: No PE since February because of comments about his feet and his weight in the changing room, which got onto a group chat with photos. Dreads school; has missed some days by saying he was ill. Low mood most days for about two months, no enjoyment, poor sleep, tired, eating more junk.

Sometimes thinks people would be better off without him. No plans, never acted on it, no self-harm, no previous attempts. Would not want to upset his younger sister. Paracetamol is in the kitchen cupboard. No drugs; a few beers at a friend’s once a month.
Does not want Mum to know about the photos or the thoughts: “She’ll go mental at the school.” Would be okay with her knowing he is “feeling down” and that he needs some help.

Monosyllabic while Mum is there. Opens up if the doctor explains confidentiality simply and asks about school and friends without judgement. Relieved to be asked. Agrees to a plan if he has a say in what Mum is told.

ice.ideas: (Mum) “Athlete’s foot, and he’s lazy about washing.” (Callum, alone) “It’s my feet that started all of it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: Callum is being humiliated online, is low and has passive thoughts that people would be better off without him; he is frightened his mother will make it worse at school.
ice.expectations: (Mum) “Something stronger, maybe tablets.” (Callum) “For it to stop.”

cues: A teenager who has stopped showering, gaming till 3am and quit football — self-neglect and withdrawal are cues, not just laziness.
Hood up, no eye contact, one-word answers while Mum talks — ask to see him alone.
“It’s my feet that started all of it” — the bullying behind the skin complaint.
“What’s the point” — ask directly about suicidal thoughts.

checkpoints.text: Confirms tinea pedis (interdigital maceration and fissuring), checks for cellulitis, nail involvement and how the previous cream was used

Treats appropriately: a topical antifungal such as terbinafine or an imidazole for the recommended duration (check the SPC/local formulary), with practical foot hygiene; does not offer oral treatment for uncomplicated interdigital disease
Notices the self-neglect and withdrawal as cues and asks to speak with Callum alone, explaining confidentiality and its limits
Takes a HEADSS-style history (home, education, activities, drugs and alcohol, sexuality as relevant, suicide and mood) and identifies bullying and low mood
Asks directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, self-harm, protective factors and access to means; judges current risk

Plans support for depression in a young person in line with NICE NG134 (for example guided self-help or digital CBT, school support, referral to CAMHS or the local mental health support team as appropriate, early review)
Agrees with Callum what will be shared with his mother, and a safety plan including crisis contacts and safe storage of medicines
Engages a reluctant adolescent respectfully, avoids blaming him or his mother, and brings the mother back in constructively

worked.txt: “This is athlete’s foot. The cream only works if it goes on every day for the full course, even after it looks better. Dry between the toes, clean socks every day, and let the trainers dry out between wears.”
“Callum, I like to speak to young people on their own for part of the appointment, it’s routine. Jo, would you mind stepping out for a few minutes? I’ll bring you back in.”
“What you tell me stays between us, unless I’m worried you or someone else is at serious risk. If that happened, I’d talk to you first about who needs to know.”
“How are things at school at the moment? And with your mates?”
“When things feel that bad, some people have thoughts of ending their life or that people would be better off without them. Have you had thoughts like that?”
“What would you be happy for me to tell your mum? Could we say that you’ve been feeling low and we’re getting you some help, and leave the details for you to share when you’re ready?”

f.learning: A skin complaint can be a young person’s ticket of entry. Tinea pedis is common and easy to treat: interdigital itch, maceration, scaling and fissuring, usually between the 4th and 5th toes. NICE CKS recommends a topical antifungal (for example terbinafine for 1–2 weeks or an imidazole for several weeks, depending on the product; check the SPC/local formulary) plus foot hygiene: dry between the toes, change socks daily, alternate footwear, and do not share towels. Most “treatment failures” are short or irregular use. Oral antifungals are not needed for uncomplicated interdigital infection. The real station is the cue: a 16-year-old who has stopped washing, games through the night, has quit his team and will not look at the camera. Self-neglect and withdrawal should prompt a psychosocial history. See the young person alone for part of the consultation, explain confidentiality and its limits, and use a HEADSS framework. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, self-harm, protective factors and access to means; asking does not increase risk. NICE NG134 (Depression in children and young people) supports watchful waiting, then psychological therapy such as digital CBT, group or individual CBT, with referral to CAMHS for moderate to severe depression or risk. Bullying, including online, should be addressed with the school with the young person’s agreement. Agree with him what will be shared with his parent, and give a safety plan and crisis contacts. A 16-year-old is presumed to have capacity to consent, and his confidentiality should be respected unless there is a serious risk of harm (GMC 0–18 years guidance).

points.t: Interdigital itch, maceration, scaling and fissuring. Treat with a topical antifungal for the full recommended course and continue after the skin looks clear (check the SPC/local formulary) [1,5].
Dry carefully between the toes, cotton socks changed daily, alternate shoes so they dry out, flip-flops in communal showers, do not share towels.
Spreading redness, swelling or fever (cellulitis), nail involvement (needs confirmation before oral treatment), or diabetes or immunosuppression.
Routine for adolescents. Explain why, ask the parent to step out, and explain confidentiality and its limits [4].
Home, Education/employment, Activities, Drugs and alcohol, Sexuality, Suicide and mood (plus Safety). Start with less sensitive areas.
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, self-harm, protective factors and access to means. Do not use risk tools or scores to predict risk; focus on needs and a safety plan [3].

NICE NG134: for mild depression, watchful waiting with review and digital CBT, group CBT or group non-directive supportive therapy; for moderate to severe depression, refer to CAMHS for psychological therapy. Antidepressants are not offered in primary care without specialist assessment [2].
With his agreement, involve the school (pastoral lead or mental health support team). Online image sharing may need the school’s safeguarding lead.

dg.d: Open question; heard the mother, then asked Callum in his own words.
HEADSS seen alone: school, PE and the group chat, friends, football, sleep, gaming, alcohol, family.
Remote look between the toes; no tests needed for typical tinea pedis; mood assessed; no physical cause for low mood suggested.
Tinea pedis versus pitted keratolysis or eczema; low mood and depression versus adjustment to bullying; substance use.
Cellulitis features; suicidal thoughts, plans, self-harm, means and protective factors.
Tinea pedis inadequately treated; low mood consistent with depression in the context of bullying, with passive suicidal thoughts and no plans.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Topical antifungal for the full course with foot hygiene (check the SPC/local formulary); support for low mood in line with NICE NG134; safety plan and crisis contacts; review in 1–2 weeks.
Bullying and image sharing: agreed approach to involving the school; sleep and gaming; medicines stored safely at home.
Review booked; crisis routes (SHOUT, Childline, 999); agreed what Mum is told; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Self-neglect, withdrawal, hood up and silence with Mum present; “what’s the point”.
Mum: athlete’s foot and laziness, wants something stronger. Callum: the feet started the bullying; wants it to stop; fears Mum will make it worse.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Callum is being humiliated online, is low and has passive thoughts that people would be better off without him; he is frightened his mother will make it worse at school — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Hi Callum, and you must be Mum. What’s been going on?
(Mum) It’s his feet. They stink the house out, the skin’s peeling, and the cream from the chemist did nothing. He needs something stronger. And he won’t listen to a word I say.
Callum, can you tell me about your feet in your own words? What bothers you most?
(Callum) Itchy. Between my toes.
How long has it been going on, and how often did you use the cream?
(Callum) Couple of months. Used it twice. Then I lost it.
Any redness spreading up your foot, swelling, feeling feverish, or changes in your toenails?
model.why: Screens for cellulitis and nail disease

model.text: (Callum) No.
Could you show me between your toes on the camera? Thanks. That white, soggy, cracked skin between the little toes is typical of athlete’s foot. No spreading redness. That’s good.
(Mum) He wears the same socks for days. And he hardly showers now. He’s up gaming till 3am and he’s given up football.
Thanks, that’s helpful. Callum, I usually talk to young people on their own for part of the appointment, it’s routine. Jo, would you mind stepping out for a few minutes? I’ll bring you back in.
model.why: Notices cues; arranges to see alone

model.text: (Mum) Fine. (leaves)
Callum, what you say to me stays between us, unless I’m worried that you or someone else is at serious risk. If that happened, I’d talk to you first about who needs to know. Is that okay?
(Callum) Yeah.
How are things at school at the moment?
(Callum) Rubbish. I don’t do PE any more. Someone took a picture of my feet in the changing room and put it on the group chat. And they say stuff about my weight.
That sounds really humiliating. I’m sorry that happened. How has it been affecting you?
(Callum) I don’t want to go in. I’ve said I was ill a few times. I just game. Nothing’s fun any more. What’s the point.
How long have you felt like that? How are you sleeping and eating, and how is your energy?
(Callum) About two months. Can’t sleep. Tired all the time. Eat rubbish.
When things feel that bad, some people have thoughts that they’d be better off dead or that people would be better off without them. Have you had thoughts like that?
(Callum) Sometimes. That they’d be better off without me. I wouldn’t do anything. My little sister…
Thank you for telling me. Have you ever hurt yourself, or made any plans? Is there anything at home you’ve thought about using?
(Callum) No. Never. There’s just paracetamol in the kitchen.
Any drugs, or drinking?
(Callum) A few beers at a mate’s sometimes. No drugs.

It sounds like you’ve been feeling low for a couple of months, and the bullying is a big part of that. That’s something we can help with. I’d like to get you some talking support, there are online and school-based options, and I’d like to see you again in a week or two. If it gets worse, we’d involve the young people’s mental health team.
model.why: Explains low mood and plan (NICE NG134)

model.text: (Callum) Don’t tell Mum about the photos. She’ll go mental at the school.

What would you be happy for me to tell her? Could we say you’ve been feeling down and we’re getting you some help, and you tell her the rest when you’re ready? I do think the school needs to know about the photos, but we can talk about how and when, together.
(Callum) Yeah. That’s okay.
And if those thoughts ever get stronger, you can call me, text SHOUT on 85258, call Childline, or ring 999. Could the paracetamol be kept somewhere you can’t easily get to for now?

Jo, thanks for waiting. Callum’s feet: the cream needs using every day for the full course on the pack, even once it looks better, with clean socks daily and trainers dried out. I’ll prescribe it. Callum’s also told me he’s been feeling quite down lately, and we’ve agreed some support. I’ll see him again in a week or two.
(Mum) Down? I thought he was just being lazy.

It’s really common for low mood to look like that from the outside. The most helpful thing you can do is keep things calm and let him talk when he’s ready. And keep medicines locked away for now. Callum, can you tell me the plan back?
(Callum) Cream every day till it’s gone. Clean socks. Online help. Come back in two weeks. Call if it gets worse.

social.t: Images shared on group chats follow young people home. Withdrawal, school avoidance and self-neglect are common responses.
Parents often read low mood as laziness. Helping them understand reduces conflict at home.

legal.t: A 16-year-old is presumed to have capacity. Respect his confidentiality unless there is a serious risk of harm, and involve him in decisions about sharing (GMC 0–18 years).
Sharing intimate or humiliating images of a child can be a safeguarding and criminal matter; schools have procedures, coordinated by the designated safeguarding lead.

professional.t: Asking directly does not increase risk. Focus on needs and a safety plan rather than a risk score (NICE NG225).
Treat the presenting complaint well, but follow the cues that suggest something more.

community.t: Many schools have mental health support teams and pastoral leads who can offer low-intensity support and act on bullying.
SHOUT (text 85258), Childline (0800 1111), Papyrus HOPELINE247, NHS 111 (mental health option) and 999.

redFlags: Suicidal plans, intent, preparation or self-harm: same-day CAMHS/crisis assessment
Spreading redness, swelling or fever from the foot: cellulitis
Drug use, school refusal with safeguarding concerns, or abuse: safeguarding discussion
ice: Mum: athlete’s foot and laziness; wants something stronger
Callum: the feet started the bullying; wants it to stop
Callum: fears Mum will make it worse at school

playbook.diagnosis: “Your feet have athlete’s foot that hasn’t had a proper go with the cream. And you’ve been feeling low for a couple of months, with the bullying behind a lot of it.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Athlete’s foot is a fungus that loves warm, damp skin. It clears if the cream is used every day for the whole course and the feet are kept dry. Feeling low like this is common and it does get better with the right help.”

management.reflectIce: “Mum wanted something stronger for the feet; you wanted the bullying to stop and not to make things worse. We can do both.”
management.psychosocial: Agreed message to Mum; school involvement with Callum’s agreement; sleep routine; football as a goal.
sharedPlan: Topical antifungal daily for the full course on the pack (check the SPC/local formulary); foot hygiene
Low mood: guided self-help or digital CBT, school mental health support; CAMHS referral if moderate to severe or risk increases (NICE NG134)
Safety plan: crisis contacts; medicines stored safely
School approached about the image sharing, agreed with Callum
safetyNet: Thoughts of ending his life getting stronger, any plan or self-harm: call the practice, SHOUT 85258, Childline, NHS 111 or 999
Spreading redness, swelling or fever from the foot
No improvement in the skin after the full course

pitfalls.intro: Prescribing for athlete’s foot takes a minute. The station tests whether you notice a withdrawn teenager, see him alone and ask about risk.

items.why: The cream was used twice; interdigital tinea responds to a full topical course.
items.fix: Explain correct use and duration; add foot hygiene.

items.why: He will not disclose in front of his mother.
items.fix: Make seeing alone routine and explain confidentiality.

items.why: Self-neglect and withdrawal are cues to low mood.
He has passive thoughts and access to paracetamol.
items.fix: Ask directly; plans, self-harm, means, protective factors.

items.why: Either breaks trust or leaves him unsupported.
items.fix: Agree with Callum what will be shared.

items.why: Depression in young people needs early review.
items.fix: Review in 1–2 weeks with clear crisis routes.

Duration, cream use, cellulitis and nails; look on camera. Note the self-neglect.
Confidentiality. HEADSS: school, bullying, mood, sleep, drugs. Direct risk questions and means.
Low mood support (NG134); school; what Mum will be told; safety plan.
Foot treatment and hygiene; agreed mood message; medicines stored safely; teach-back; review.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a stronger antifungal, or tablets, and ends the consultation; never sees Callum alone; treats the self-neglect as laziness; no risk assessment.
wordPics.pass: Treats the tinea correctly, sees Callum alone, uncovers bullying and low mood, asks about suicidal thoughts and plans support.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains confidentiality and its limits clearly; uses HEADSS naturally; gives a safety plan with crisis contacts and means restriction; negotiates exactly what Mum will be told; supports Mum without blaming; arranges early review and a route to the school.

avoid.instead: “The cream needs using every day for the whole course. Let’s do that properly.”
avoid.why: Most failures are short use; oral antifungals are not needed for interdigital tinea.

avoid.instead: “I usually see young people on their own for part of the appointment.”
avoid.why: Disclosure is unlikely in front of a parent.

avoid.instead: “Have you had thoughts of ending your life or that people would be better off without you?”
avoid.why: Closed, leading questions shut down disclosure.

Parents often read low mood as laziness. Helping them understand reduces conflict at home.

legal.t: A 16-year-old is presumed to have capacity. Respect his confidentiality unless there is a serious risk of harm, and involve him in decisions about sharing (GMC 0–18 years).
Sharing intimate or humiliating images of a child can be a safeguarding and criminal matter; schools have procedures, coordinated by the designated safeguarding lead.

professional.t: Asking directly does not increase risk. Focus on needs and a safety plan rather than a risk score (NICE NG225).
Treat the presenting complaint well, but follow the cues that suggest something more.

community.t: Many schools have mental health support teams and pastoral leads who can offer low-intensity support and act on bullying.
SHOUT (text 85258), Childline (0800 1111), Papyrus HOPELINE247, NHS 111 (mental health option) and 999.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Athlete’s foot is a fungus that loves warm, damp skin. It clears if the cream is used every day for the whole course and the feet are kept dry. Feeling low like this is common and it does get better with the right help.”
